To make things related to the sanitization topic clearer, we need to be sure that sanitization as a defense is an acceptable option for the current data or process.

I think it would be good to have a requirement in "V1.1 Encoding and Sanitization Architecture" (preferred) or in "V1.3 Sanitization" to say:

> Verify that if sanitization is chosen as a defense method, it is accepted by "business logic rules" to make automatic modifications to the input, as changing the data removes data integrity.

The wording should be improved, hopefully it it is good enough to explain the idea.

One option is also to move to the documented security decisions with this.

comments.body:
I was thinking something very similar in response to [your comment here](https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/3335#issuecomment-4016016341), so I'm very glad to see you came up with the same idea.

A couple of nuances:
- Would prefer it to be part of [V1.3 Sanitization](https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/blob/master/5.0/en/0x10-V1-Encoding-and-Sanitization.md#v13-sanitization), and even specifically 1.3.1, as a codified prerequisite to other sanitization requirements.
- Would avoid mentioning business logic or other implications that may lead to the decision being taken by non-experts with the wrong incentives, such as project managers or product owners. Instead, I'd lean on the last resort warning.

Not great wording, just an example of what I mean:
> Verify that if sanitization is used, all defense mechanisms that would preserve data integrity have been determined to be inapplicable, and sanitization is only applied to data that wouldn't propagate further than immediate use.

I would not limit it to immediate use,.iI needed there can be additional clause to point that "full flow need to be analyzed" or something like that.

For example, most likely WYSIWYG content can be sanitized and also saved as sanitized. It can be done to anything else, if the "business logic" has decided that it is ok to do so (automatically change user-input).

I'm happy to explain the entire concept, the reasons for current solution, detected and known areas that can be improved. But I would not like to have another issue with the demagogy madness here. So in case you have found your way into Slack, ping me there.

I'm ok to iterate without the immediate use limitation at least for now, it's not the main point. Are you happy with the rest of my rationale? i.e. framing as all other options are exhausted instead of business is ok with it.

I do not think “accepted by business logic rules” is the right framing for a general HTML sanitization requirement. The core question should be whether sanitization is an appropriate and technically justified control for that specific data flow and sink, not whether non-security stakeholders are comfortable with automatic modification of input.

For example, in the case of untrusted HTML rendered in a browser, sanitization is of course the primary security control for preventing XSS. The important issue is whether a robust HTML sanitizer is used, not whether business logic has approved modification of the input.

So I would recommend framing this around suitability of sanitization for the specific context, interpreter, and downstream use, rather than around business rules.

> I do not think “accepted by business logic rules” is the right framing for a general HTML sanitization requirement.

How "untrusted HTML" (input from WYSIWYG) should be sanitized is very much a "business logical and documentation" question, as one need to define and accept, which tags are accepted (which functionality HTML should provide).

> Are you happy with the rest of my rationale? i.e. framing as all other options are exhausted instead of business is ok with it.

> all defense mechanisms that would preserve data integrity have been determined to be inapplicable

I'm not sure we need this (applicable/inapplicable condition) in the requirement; it feels like something to be in the section text. It also raises a philosophical question: how to measure - is there an alternative to sanitization or not? With that, I think we enter the application logic area here, and we should not dictate the functionality for the application. I think just asking a security decision to be made for each sanitization use case should do the job.

Here was the target "functional data-field" that comes from the user, that can (and must) be analyzed and documented. But there can also be technical needs that need to keep things safe "deep in the flow" or "deep in the program code". Those can not be targeted to be documented the same way as user-input fields are.

It is important to understand the difference between those and avoid mixing them.

> How "untrusted HTML" (input from WYSIWYG) should be sanitized is very much a "business logical and documentation" question, as one need to define and accept, which tags are accepted (which functionality HTML should provide).

That has absolutely zero impact on whether this is a security control. **_Using a proper HTML sanitizer stops injection_**. Your HTML sanitization rules define allowed functionality; they do not change the fact that sanitization is the security control.

> they do not change the fact that sanitization is the security control

Anyone have said that sanitization is not a security control? Just stop this (inventing random statements like someone has stated the fact X and then you come and oppose it). Otherwise there is another issue full of noise, demagogy, invented "facts" etc.

> Anyone have said that sanitization is not a security control? Just stop this (inventing random statements like someone has stated the fact X and then you come and oppose it). Otherwise there is another issue full of noise, demagogy, invented "facts" etc.

I think this is conflating _governance_ with _security control effectiveness_.

HTML sanitization is itself a security control. A mature sanitizer such as DOMPurify, used correctly, can provide strong security value even without a separately published business policy defining every rule in advance. And "used correctly" does not mean configuration, it just needs to be used in client code where frameworks do not have sanitization built-in like Angular.

A documented policy may help consistency and maintenance, but it is not required for sanitization to function as a valid security control.

Now if you want to set a "business policy" that HTML Sanitizers like DOMPurify needs to be used on the client, I would back that.

> I'm not sure we need this (applicable/inapplicable condition) in the requirement; it feels like something to be in the section text.

I guess I was mistaken about having the same idea then. Throughout all related arguments, my biggest concern has always been that section text clarifications are not as prominent as hard requirements, which effectively demotes any warnings.

> @elarlang Is this requirement being written primarily with HTML sanitization in mind, or is it intended to cover other forms of sanitization as well? 

It is meant to be general.

> > I'm not sure we need this (applicable/inapplicable condition) in the requirement; it feels like something to be in the section text.
> 
> I guess I was mistaken about having the same idea then. Throughout all related arguments, my biggest concern has always been that section text clarifications are not as prominent as hard requirements, which effectively demotes any warnings.

There is also a chance that we talk about the same thing but call it differently.

So the question to solve with this requirement is - who and in which condition decides, that using a sanitization in that situation is ok or not. My point was, that we can not dictate the application logic and decide can they use sanitization instead of validation.

When sanitization comes into the picture, changes are by default, so what is the sense of drafting a new requirement?

When sanitization is applied, the data is intentionally changed to remove malicious content, and this transformation is part of the security control.

Do Security frameworks do require business approval for encoding or sanitization?

> When sanitization comes into the picture, changes are by default, so what is the sense of drafting a new requirement?

If something is making "changes by default" into your input that you are not aware of, it is quite problematic I guess.

Yes, it may provide defense against injections etc, and we are going to the ruining the integrity area here again.

As I wrote in my previous comment:
> So the question to solve with this requirement is - who and in which condition decides, that using a sanitization in that situation is ok or not.

>  we are going to the ruining the integrity area here again

Sanitization intentionally modifies input to make it safe. This modification is part of the security control. So `ruining the integrity` is misleading,

> So the question to solve with this requirement is - who and in which condition decides, that using a sanitization in that situation is ok or not.

There is already a separate “Sanitization” section, so the relevant requirements for when sanitization should be used. I do not see why an additional requirement is needed, especially one framed around “**business logic rules**” and **loss of integrity**.

> Sanitization intentionally modifies input to make it safe

Please provide examples, which kind of situation you keep in mind.

> So ruining the integrity is misleading,

Obviously, I don't agree with this one.

> There is already a separate “Sanitization” section, so the relevant requirements for when sanitization should be used. I do not see why an additional requirement is needed, especially one framed around “business logic rules” and loss of integrity.

You can ignore the "business logic" if that causes an allergy.

The difference between input validation and sanitization is rejection vs modification. My abstract point is that ASVS should not dictate which needs to be used in each case, but this is up to the application owner to decide whether modifying the data is accepted/suitable or not.

The goal is to avoid using sanitization when it was not decided as an acceptable solution (as auto-modification to the data and ruining the integrity was not accepted) AND allow sanitization even other options are available, but it is accepted process.

The current section text for sanitization (it is debated separately, it will be updated, and for everyone - please do not duplicate this discussion here):

> The ideal protection against using untrusted content in an unsafe context is to use context-specific encoding or escaping, which maintains the same semantic meaning of the unsafe content but renders it safe for use in that particular context, as discussed in more detail in the previous section.

> Where this is not possible, sanitization becomes necessary, removing potentially dangerous characters or content. In some cases, this may change the semantic meaning of the input, but for security reasons, there may be no alternative.

So, here is kind of requirement written into the section text - "that if nothing else is allowed, you can use sanitization."

I would open it up with the requirement to "it is allowed when it is decided application functionality or flow", even, in theory there are other options (encoding, validation) available.

But again, as it changes the data and it's integrity, then by principle it must be accepted behavior.

> Please provide examples, which kind of situation you keep in mind.

Example I had in mind: html, logs, files, css, etc.

> Obviously, I don't agree with this one.

Could you please explain why?

> The goal is to avoid using sanitization when it was not decided as an acceptable solution

ASVS is a security verification standard, not an architecture or design decision guide.

> (as auto-modification to the data and ruining the integrity was not accepted)

Could you provide some concrete use cases where sanitization would be considered unacceptable due to integrity concerns?

> that if nothing else is allowed, you can use sanitization.

Could you clarify what scenarios you have in mind here?

> But again, as it changes the data and it's integrity, then by principle it must be accepted behavior.

Could you please share what you mean by “**integrity**” in web security, and how you think sanitization affects it?

> > Obviously, I don't agree with this one.

> Could you please explain why?

Regarding explanation on the "integrity", I don't really have anything to add to my previous comment. I feel everything was explained there and I'm already looping a bit here.

> ASVS is a security verification standard, not an architecture or design decision guide.

You can not verify is "using the sanitization is correct" or not, if you don't have security decisions made on that.

> Could you provide some concrete use cases where sanitization would be considered unacceptable due to integrity concerns?
> Could you clarify what scenarios you have in mind here?

By default, it should not be used anywhere, if it is not accepted and understood behavior.

> Could you please share what you mean by “integrity” in web security, and how you think sanitization affects it?

Abstractly, the data is kept and handled exactly as it came from the source. The source can be an end-user, via API, from wherever the application gets the input.

> You can not verify is "using the sanitization is correct" or not, if you don't have security decisions made on that. Security decisions are already covered based upon the documentation section. > You can not verify is "using the sanitization is correct" or not, if you don't have security decisions made on that. > By default, it should not be used anywhere, if it is not accepted and understood behavior. This is applicable to each functional process of the application, it's not just related to sanitization, for example: **basic numeric check validation should not be used anywhere until and unless it is accepted and understood behavior, so how is sanitization different?** > Abstractly, the data is kept and handled exactly as it came from the source. The source can be an end-user, via API, from wherever the application gets the input. [NIST](https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/data_integrity) and [OWASP ](https://devguide.owasp.org/en/02-foundations/01-security-fundamentals/#integrity) define integrity as protection against unauthorized modification. Sanitization is an authorized security control and as per the official definition, it is not an integrity violation. here are the written text screenshot: ### NIST ### OWASP Dev Guide **Note: The end-user submitting malicious input is not a legitimate data modification.**

> > You can not verify is "using the sanitization is correct" or not, if you don't have security decisions made on that.

> Security decisions are already covered based upon the documentation section.

Which requirement covers that?

> basic numeric check validation should not be used anywhere until and unless it is accepted and understood behavior, so how is sanitization different?

It is defined by 2.1.1 + 2.2.1. When you can or can not use sanitization is not covered by security decision requirement.

> Sanitization **is an authorized security** control and as per the official definition, it is not an integrity violation.

Boom. And who gave the authorization to random component to modify the data?

And that is the reason why I propose to have the requirement. You can sanitize whatever, if it is decided to do so. So, in a way, I can not understand what you are fighting against.

I have answered the questions in good faith and put a lot of effort into it. I'm not convinced that the good faith is not misused here.

Or let me ask it another way: do you state that sanitization is always ok to use because it is a security control with a goal to make data safe?

> I have answered the questions in good faith and put a lot of effort into it. I'm not convinced that the good faith is not misused here.

I appreciate the effort you have put into this discussion, and I am engaging in good faith. Based on my experience from our discussions across multiple tickets, I strongly believe that your intention is always to make ASVS better, and I truly respect that. Please don’t assume otherwise.

If you still feel that I am not engaging in good faith, I am happy to stop the discussion here.

I may be wrong in several areas, please feel free to correct me.


> Or let me ask it another way: do you state that sanitization is always ok to use because it is a security control with a goal to make data safe?

No, sanitization is not always OK blindly in every context. The position is when sanitization is the appropriate control for a given context, applying it is not an integrity violation.


I will answer your other questions but let first conclude the discussion "data integrity", shall I assume you agree that data integrity is not an issue with sanitization, so we can close that part of the discussion and focus on the remaining points?

> No, sanitization is not always OK blindly in every context.

I agree with that sentense.

> The position is when sanitization is the appropriate control for a given context , applying it is not an integrity violation.

I also agree with that sentense.

But for some reason you don't want to see, that the proposed requirement is for deciding, is the situation "appropriate control for a given context" or not. That is it.

And if it is approved, it changes the integrity, but it is accepted behavior. That is why the requirement is needed - to decide, is it expected or is it integrity violation.

---

> I will answer your other questions but let first conclude the discussion "data integrity", shall I assume you agree that data integrity is not an issue with sanitization, so we can close that part of the discussion and focus on the remaining points?

By definition and impact sanitization is clear integrity killer, as it modifies the data. So after sanitization integrity is gone, and my point is, this must be approved, agreed and analyzed decision.

I really don't like the AI-festival I have seen in some issues, but for smooth wording, I used "define data integrity" in Google search and AI overview section says something I agree with:

> Data integrity refers to the accuracy, consistency, and reliability of data throughout its entire lifecycle, ensuring it remains trustworthy, unaltered, and valid. It guarantees that data is not compromised by errors, hacks, or system failures during storage, **transfer, or usage**.

And selected lines from "Key Aspects of Data Integrity:""

> Consistency: Data remains uniform across different tables, applications, and systems.
> Reliability: Data remains stable and trustworthy over time.

My assumption is that you may ignore aspects, that integrity must stay also during transfer and usage. Everywhere and always.

What we see from @elarlang is what I feel to be demagoguery and strictness that makes no sense and is not inline with normal security standards.

If every transformation were considered an integrity violation, then the following would also be “integrity killers”:

- canonicalization
- normalization
- encoding
- compression
- schema validation
- trimming whitespace
- converting character sets
- parsing JSON into objects

All of these modify the original byte sequence, yet none are considered integrity violations.

> What we see from @elarlang is what I feel to be demagoguery and strictness that makes no sense and is not inline with normal security standards.

In this conversation, I would like to say that both are contributing in good faith. I try to explain my position and answer all the questions. I also think that there is no difference in supporting the concept, but I can not be sure till we are there or we are not.

So for sure, there is no demagoguery here, there is no strictness here. It is a proposal for a requirement, and to have a discussion for that, it is expected behavior.

But for sure, we can not say that you came here with good faith to contribute to it. You choose a personal attack instead. So I kindly ask you not to ruin yet another discussion.

For the rest of your comment, I recommend to carefully read and analyze the issue first.
Fair enough @elarlang - I'll back off this thread and let you both resolve it.

> AI overview section says something I agree with:

> >Data integrity refers to the accuracy, consistency, and reliability of data throughout its entire lifecycle, ensuring it remains trustworthy, unaltered, and valid. It guarantees that data is not compromised by errors, hacks, or system failures during storage, transfer, or usage.

> And selected lines from "Key Aspects of Data Integrity:""

> > Consistency: Data remains uniform across different tables, applications, and systems.
> > Reliability: Data remains stable and trustworthy over time.

So what your cited definition says that integrity protects against errors, hacks, and system failures and key aspects are consistency and reliability. None of these are violated by sanitization. Sanitized data is more consistent and more reliable across systems than unsanitized malicious input. **Your cited agreement supports my data integrity concern**:

* **Trustworthy** : sanitized data is more trustworthy.
* **hacks** : sanitization prevents compromise by hacks.
* **Reliability** : sanitized data is more reliable for its intended use.
* **Errors & System Failures**": No where role of sanitization in this.
* **Consistency** : consistent for appropriate context.

So after reading your cited text I can firmly say that sanitization enforces integrity not integrity killer.

 
> So after sanitization integrity is gone, and my point is, this must be approved, agreed and analyzed decision

If ASVS needs a integrity acceptance requirement for sanitization because it modifies data. Then I would suggest we should think in broader aspect and add a universal requirement which covers all modern cases related to the data integrity. Let me explain why and I would suggest to draft a requirement to cover all type of edge cases.

As I think data transformation is a fundamental and unavoidable part of how applications work. Data changes form constantly as it moves through layers from client to server, server to database, database to output. This is not integrity violation, this is normal application behavior. Here I am sharing few of the cases :

Transformation | Data Change |  Integrity Requirement Needed? 
-- | --| --|
 a user enters a numeric value in a text input field, and the application stores it in the database as an INT data type instead of a string. The representation changed, the type changed, but this is not considered an integrity violation| Yes (type change) | No, It's functional decision
File stored as Base64 instead of bytes  | Yes | No, It's encoding decision
Date format converted client > server >DB | Yes | No, It's format decision
< encoded to &lt; for HTML output  | Yes | No it's security control
JSON normalized before DB storage | Yes | No it's storage decision
Image resized/compressed on upload  | Yes | No it's functional decision
Phone number normalized to E.164 format  | Yes | No it's validation decision
Whitespace trimmed from user input  | Yes | No it's processing decision
Unicode normalized for storage  | Yes | No it's encoding decision
HTML sanitization removing <script>  | Yes | No it's security control

**Every single one of these modifies user data.** if data-integrity highlights only for sanitization then we would need separate integrity-acceptance for each of them and that is clearly unworkable as demonstrated above.

None of the cited definitions, including NIST, OWASP, or the AI overview you referenced, state that client-received data is the main source of truth that must be preserved as it is.

**Your governance concern is valid** but scope of the proposed wording is not aligned with the normal application behavior. I would suggest we should draft the requirement as below and it should be listed somewhere under Business Documentation section.

**Verify that data transformation decisions including sanitization, encoding, and format conversion are documented as intentional architectural decisions.**

The list you provided needs quite some analysis one by one, as there is mixing, fully converting the entire input to another format with a reversible option, and changing the actual input.

But I would get clarification first to the main question (in my opinion), in [your comment](https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/3346#issuecomment-4048912182) you wrote:

> No, sanitization is not always OK blindly in every context. The position is that when sanitization is the appropriate control for a given context, applying it is not an integrity violation.

You agree, that sanitization needs to be authorized and approved to make changes to the input.

The question is: where, why, and who decides it, is it authorized and approved?

> Trustworthy : sanitized data is more trustworthy.

No it isn't. It may be "safer" from your POV thinking primarily of injection prevention, but that is only one side to it.

What if the data was meant to be code, and you stripped a key part of it?
What if ``#1234`` was an identifier that the user tried to communicate, but an aggressive sanitizer erased it? (something that I've seen happen)
What if you sanitize out a part of someone's physical address meant for shipping?
What if you mangle something legally-registered as is?

I don't understand the comparisons to benign operations like base64 encoding, which perfectly preserve the original data. Sanitization is inherently violating data integrity because it **destroys** part of the data, which changes its meaning.

Btw, this does include image resizing - images have metadata that you are stripping. Some of them even contain digital signatures meant to satisfy a security goal. Similarly, sanitizing logs can be damaging audit trails.

Just because a security concern can, with all context considered, justify an integrity violation, that doesn't make it not an integrity violation and saying that "sanitization enforces integrity" is absurd.

> The question is: where, why, and who decides it, is it authorized and approved?

where, why, and who are already answered in my last comment of the proposed requirement:

"**Verify that data transformation decisions including sanitization, encoding, and format conversion are documented as intentional architectural decisions.**"

"**Architectural decisions**" covers where and who. "**Documented**" covers why. verifying it would confirm that the decision was made intentionally, by the right person, at the right level.

> The list you provided needs quite some analysis one by one

Will wait for your feedback.

I think we are not in sync with the term "integrity" and the comment from @narfbg supports that understanding.

I have said it multiple times that sanitization by concept is an integrity killer as it changes the data.

For example, encoding and compressing are used to transfer data with its full content to another format, which is necessary to present it for the interpreter in use. This does not kill the integrity of the presentation. Sure, you can come here with whataboutism and find scenarios, is it ok in this case, and is it ok in that case, and we need to watch them one by one.

But, trimming a whitespace is already against integrity. Often, whitespace is trimmed from user input, and it does not cause any other problem, but if we need to measure the data integrity and make a hash-checksum of it, it is changed.

> where, why, and who are already answered in my last comment of the proposed requirement:

> Verify that data transformation decisions including sanitization, encoding, and format conversion are documented as intentional architectural decisions.

If those examples are understandable for you, then you may understand that sanitization does not belong to the "data transformation" area and can not be seen as encoding.

I still would like to ask [the question](https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/3346#issuecomment-4053476164) again.

> > Trustworthy : sanitized data is more trustworthy.

> No it isn't. It may be "safer" from your POV thinking primarily of injection prevention, but that is only one side to it.

The "**trustworthy**" point was made specifically in the context where sanitization is the appropriate and correctly scoped control. When a user submits malicious HTML in a field that will be rendered in a browser, sanitizing it produces data that is more trustworthy for its intended purpose, that is not an integrity violation, it is integrity enforcement in the correct context.

> I don't understand the comparisons to benign operations like base64 encoding, which perfectly preserve the original data.

I think there is a misunderstanding about the purpose of the table. Those 10 examples were not presented as comparisons to sanitization, they were presented to demonstrate that data transformation is a fundamental and unavoidable part of normal application behavior.


Your examples of #1234 being stripped or an address being mangled are not cases of sanitization being the appropriate control, they are cases of sanitization being incorrectly scoped or misapplied

> Sanitization is inherently violating data integrity because it destroys part of the data, which changes its meaning.

Wait for sometime for the conclusion on violating data integrity part.

> When a user submits malicious HTML in a field that will be rendered in a browser, sanitizing it produces data that is more trustworthy for its intended purpose, that is not an integrity violation, it is integrity enforcement in the correct context.

Oh, no, @ajayojha - in the context of data integrity, the "trustworthy" means that not a single bit of the data is changed. You apply "I can use it safely in the HTML output" to "trustworthy". Those are completely different things.

I think all important pieces are discussed in the issue. I recommend taking a bit of a timeout here, investigating the data integrity concept, and not only from the pieces that could support your current agenda, but from the "blank page point of view".

> ... examples of https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/pull/1234 being stripped or an address being mangled are not cases of sanitization being the appropriate control, they are cases of sanitization being incorrectly scoped or misapplied

So you basically say yourself, that there is a need to have a decision somewhere that decides, what is appropriate and what is not.

> I recommend taking a timeout and investigating data integrity from a blank page point of view.

I recognize this as a dismissal move, but I will set it aside and continue with the technical discussion.

> In the context of data integrity, trustworthy means not a single bit of the data is changed.

The "**not a single bit changed**" definition has a fundamental problem, it would make routine database operations integrity violations. When JSON is stored in a relational database, the structure changes, whitespace is removed, data types are mapped, and the binary representation changes completely. When a datetime is received from a client in IST and stored in the database as UTC Unix timestamp, the bits change at every layer.
Nobody considers these integrity violations or trustworthy failure, because integrity in any practical context has never meant bit-for-bit preservation across every layer of an application. It has always meant protection against unintended, unauthorized, or wrong changes. 

Sanitization is none of those things. It is intended, authorized, and intentional. The same is true of JSON normalization, datetime conversion, and every other transformation in the table.
The "**not a single bit changed**" definition does not hold up against normal application behavior, which is precisely the point the table was demonstrating.

> So you basically say yourself, that there is a need to have a decision somewhere that decides, what is appropriate and what is not.

"**yourself, that there is a need to have a decision** " - I never been in dispute and my disagreement has always been about the framing integrity violation. I already proposed the recommendation and your side comment is pending on that.

> I have said it multiple times that sanitization by concept is an integrity killer as it changes the data.

... and i have highlighted that not only sanitization there are other cases which also changes the data structure. one thing i like in our discussion that you have shifted from integrity violation to integrity killer.

> But, trimming a whitespace is already against integrity. Often, whitespace is trimmed from user input, and it does not cause any other problem, but if we need to measure the data integrity and make a hash-checksum of it, it is changed.

Is new requirement is required for trimming?, as this is also against the integrity.

> sanitization does not belong to the "data transformation" area and can not be seen as encoding.

Your focus is on sanitization only and I am helping you see a bigger picture rather focusing on the sanitization only. Here the objective is "Integrity Violation" it's not sanitization is belongs to the "data transformation" or not. At the end, both change data by your own definition, both would be integrity killers. So the question remains is a new requirement needed for every operation that changes a single bit?

I have reached to the point, where I feel that I'm just going to repeat myself with attempt to explain "sanitization by concept is killing the integrity as it is modifies the data". You got the [same message with explanations from](https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/3346#issuecomment-4053593445) from @narfbg .

Adding sanitization to the same list with encoding and call it "transformation" is fundamental mistake that I recommend you to analyze and reconsider the concept. Sanitization modifies the data, and modification is not a transformation.

As those understandings has not been changed, those are fundamentals to develop anything further. I have tried my best, and I don't want to put more time into it as I don't see any progress here at the moment. Yes, I know how you will interpret it.

Maybe @narfbg wants to share his vision.

Thanks @elarlang for the so far discussion with the good faith, except one dismissal move.

> Adding sanitization to the same list with encoding and call it "transformation" is fundamental mistake that I recommend you to analyze and reconsider the concept. Sanitization modifies the data, and modification is not a transformation.
 
"**modification is not a transformation**" has no basis in any technical standard. Encoding modifies data it changes its binary representation completely. Compression modifies data it reduces its size. By your own definition both would be modifications, not transformations. The distinction you are drawing does not exist every transformation involves modification, and the two terms are not mutually exclusive. 

FYI, In real-world pipelines (Spark, dbt, Airflow, Glue, etc.), sanitization is clearly part of data transformation and I would consider that modification **IS** a form of transformation.

**Encoding** — modifies data from one format to another = modification + transformation
**Compression** — modifies data by reducing size = modification + transformation
**Sanitization** — modifies data by removing harmful content = modification + transformation

@ajayojha I will attempt, once, to give you exactly what you asked for:

[OWASP definition of integrity](https://devguide.owasp.org/en/02-foundations/01-security-fundamentals/#integrity), which **you personally [cited](https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/3346#issuecomment-4046829772)**
> Integrity is about protecting data against unauthorized modification, or assuring data trustworthiness. The concept contains the notion of **data integrity (data has not been changed accidentally or deliberately)** and the notion of source integrity (data came from or was changed by a legitimate source).

[NIST definition of integrity](https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/integrity), also part of [FIPS-200](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/fips/nist.fips.200.pdf) and [SP800-53](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-53r5.pdf) (Appendix A in both documents)
> Guarding against improper information modification or destruction, and includes ensuring information non-repudiation and authenticity.

If you're going to again reply with something to the effect of _"but if sanitization is correctly scoped and intended, it's proper"_, sorry but no it isn't - **we have no clear guidance on how to decide whether it's the correct control**, which means your position has no foundation to stand on. "Technical experts" aren't the answer - anyone can claim to be that, and even the most senior ones very often make the wrong decisions.

This has been repeatedly explained already, but even when sanitization is the correct choice, that's a matter of one security concern (e.g. injection prevention) **overriding** another (integrity violation), but it doesn't make it disappear. I'll extend you an olive branch in recognizing that sanitization can be used to defend *overall* system integrity and therefore the integrity and trustworthiness of all other data in the system, which is why it is at all justifiable, but that still happens at the price of an integrity violation to a specific piece of data.

To make a more blunt analogy, if amptutating a limb is necessary to save your life, that's clearly the correct decision, yet you still lose a limb. It can be the correct decision, and it can even be reasonably argued that it preserves other limbs, but you cannot then spin that as _"amputation doesn't result in limb loss because it was the correct thing to do"_.

I also want to note that your [citation](https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/3346#issuecomment-4046829772) of [NIST on data integrity](https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/data_integrity) is based on standards in the area of cryptography and industrial control systems - fields in which sanitization simply does not exist - and the page has a clear disclaimer on its right side, which reads:
> See the identified Source document to understand each term-definition pair in its proper context.

Different standards and organizations will frame the issue differently, but all of them fundamentally mean integrity as the opposite of "damaged". This is one of the most basic concepts in security and your refusal to acknowledge it is inflammatory.
